name: Persistent Systems
summary: Persistent Systems describes itself as having a product-engineering background, and candidates commonly describe its interviews as coding-focused: an online test of aptitude, computer-science basics and coding, one or two technical interviews, and an HR round. It runs Train and Hire, a self-learning programme that prepares students for its campus hiring drive, and publishes four values: Ingenious, Confident, Responsible and Persistent.
rounds: Online assessment: aptitude, computer-science basics and coding
Technical interview: coding approach, data structures and your projects
For some roles: an advanced coding or second technical round
looks_for: Data structures and algorithms explained aloud
Working code and how you'd test it
Depth on your own project: design choices and trade-offs

questions.text: Tell me about yourself and the most technical thing you've built.
covers: Your degree or experience, briefly
The thing you built: the problem, the tech, your part
Why that kind of work is what you want to do here

questions.text: Tell me about a problem you kept working on after others had given up.
covers: The problem and why others stopped
What you tried, in order, and what finally worked
What the result made possible

questions.text: Tell me about a time you found a clever, cheaper way to get something done.
covers: The usual, costly way
Your idea and how you tested it
What it saved in time, money or effort

questions.text: Tell me about a commitment you made on a project and how you made sure you kept it.
covers: What you promised and to whom
How you planned and tracked it
What you did when something threatened it

questions.text: Tell me about a technical choice you got wrong. How did you find out?
covers: The choice and why it seemed right at the time
The sign that it was wrong
How you fixed it and what you check now before deciding

questions.text: How does a hash map work inside, and what happens when two keys collide?
covers: A hash function turns a key into a bucket index
Collisions handled by chaining or open addressing
Resizing when it gets full, and why average lookup is fast but the worst case isn't

questions.text: Talk me through how you'd detect a loop in a linked list, and the time and memory it takes.
covers: A simple approach: store visited nodes in a set, using extra memory
The two-pointer approach: a slow and a fast pointer meet if there's a loop
Time and memory for each, and how you'd test with edge cases

questions.text: What is the difference between a process and a thread, and why do threads need locks?
covers: Processes have separate memory; threads share their process's memory
Shared data can be corrupted when two threads change it at once
Locks or other tools prevent that, with the risk of deadlocks

questions.text: How would you design the back end of a simple chat app for a few thousand users?
covers: Clarifying needs: one-to-one or groups, history, online status
Main parts: a connection service (such as WebSockets), a message store, user service
Delivery to offline users and what you'd change if users grew a lot

questions.text: Explain Big O notation using a search you've written or used.
covers: What Big O describes: how time or memory grows with input size
Linear search is O(n); binary search on sorted data is O(log n)
Why the constant factors and real data sizes still matter

questions.text: Your service's response time doubled after a release. How would you find the cause?
covers: Comparing before and after: which endpoints, which users, which servers
Looking at what the release changed and at profiling or query timings
Rolling back if users are hurting, then fixing and adding a performance check

questions.text: For experienced candidates: tell me about code you reviewed and the problems you found.
covers: What the change did and what you looked for
The issues you raised: bugs, design, tests, readability
How you gave the feedback and what changed
Something specific: its product-engineering focus, a technology area or recent work
How that matches what you've built or want to build
What you'd like to learn first

questions.text: Which area do you most want to grow in: cloud, data, AI or product engineering? Why?
covers: One choice, with something you've already done in it
What draws you to it
How you're building skills there now

questions.text: Do you have any questions for us?
covers: One or two thoughtful questions about the team, the tech or the first project
Nothing already answered on the careers site
A brief thank-you

tips: Practise solving coding problems aloud: say your approach and its time and memory cost before you write code.
Revise data structures properly (arrays, linked lists, stacks, trees, hash maps); technical rounds often go beyond definitions.
If your college offers Persistent's Train and Hire programme, finish its modules before the drive.
Have one project you can go deep on: design choices, what broke, and how you'd scale it.
